title: How to Solve a Midlife Crisis with the Car You Already Have
summary: The more time I spend in my almost 50-year-old body, the more I understand why a midlife crisis is inevitable. Daily stressors have a cumulative effect, and it can get overwhelming in ways I’ve never experienced before. A release valve of some form is needed. Having accomplished most of my childhood aspirations at this point […]
body_text: The more time I spend in my almost 50-year-old body, the more I understand why a midlife crisis is inevitable. Daily stressors have a cumulative effect, and it can get overwhelming in ways I’ve never experienced before. A release valve of some form is needed. Having accomplished most of my childhood aspirations at this point in my life, I need nothing to survive and thrive. But I definitely want something. A red Corvette, an air-cooled Porsche, or a lifted 4×4? I genuinely don’t know, but I need something. Make that needed , past tense. Commissioning a graphics package from an artist for my 2011 Ford Ranger XLT resolved my impending midlife crisis. I now have a nebulous sense of excitement and satisfaction in my truck. I mean, it’s still the same old rig: honest, reliable, and downright fun to drive. But now it feels right for me in ways I cannot explain. I enjoyed the creative process even more than the finished product. This feeling can’t be replicated by a trip to a dealership, either. But my story isn’t one of self-aggrandizement or even self-reflection. Instead, it’s a tale of how to make a mass-produced vehicle into your own creation, and the lessons I learned along the way. Sajeev Mehta A custom project gets complicated when an artist has to turn a customer’s vague requests into a final product. But I had the right person for the job, and it all started with a factory photo of a 1993 Ford Ranger. The Photo That Started It All 1993 Ford Ranger XL Sport Ford Full-size American and many Toyota trucks are having a moment—values are increasing and reproduction graphics are readily available—but the second (1993–97) and third (1998–2011) generation Ford Rangers aren’t riding so high. Though there are readily available graphics if I wanted to make a Ranger Splash or STX, I initially wanted something more like the Free Wheeling graphics seen in the 1970s and in today’s Bronco and Bronco Sport. However, the Free Wheeling aesthetic isn’t correct for the 1990s-era sheetmetal found on my truck. Plus, there’s no kit designed expressly for the compact Ford Ranger. Further research of Ford-blessed graphics from 30-ish years ago was needed, and I struck gold. The iconic Jazz Cup design. Wikipedia | Gina Ekiss (design creator) | Dart Container Taco Bell. Reddit | 90s_kid The treasure was found in the 1993 Ford Ranger brochure, as the XL “Sport” model came with a Jazz disposable cup color scheme atop geometry that has the feel of a 1990s Taco Bell . The vibe probably had a short lifespan back then, but these days it’s an homage to the 1990s that delights nostalgic millennials. And that pleasure is much like the feeling I have driving my vintage 2011 Ranger in a sea of more modern trucks from the same decade. Pairing the two made sense, at least in my mind. As I have done with decades of OEM Plus upgrades, I figured it’s wise to leverage the hard work performed by the designers who get paid six-figure salaries to make these trucks in the first place. Even so, there was plenty of work ahead to reproduce long-forgotten graphics from the 1990s. I realized it would be nice to leverage a graphic designer to make it more like something available with 2010s-era technology. The Culmination Of Graphic Design Rico “Mr. Culmination” and the final product. Sajeev Mehta I used to know him as Mr. Culmination on social media, and at the end of last year we became friends at a dinner with mutual friends. His real name is Rico, and his day job is making industrial signs for corporations and commercial designs for office spaces. That résumé suggested he had the skills and the ability to implement a project. His custom Scion FR-S is a promotional billboard for his artistic talent. The more I learned about the mythical “Mr. Culmination,” the more I was sold on the content of Rico’s character. Here’s his story in his own words: “As a young boy in America, it’s difficult not to be into cool cars. However, what really turned me into a car enthusiast was the purchase of a Ferrari Enzo poster back on March 10, 2004. This happened at my elementary school’s book fair, but my intention was to get a science book. Unfortunately I needed $5 more for a book, so I used what my mom gave me to get the Ferrari poster instead. I still let my mom know that I could have been a scientist, but instead I became a car guy because of a $5 difference! Being in the car scene inspired me to design, as I wanted to create cool art for my vehicles. I’ve always loved seeing ‘modernized’ designs on retro builds. When the Ranger was presented to me, it was an easy ‘Yes, let’s do it.’ It became a very exciting part of my work that challenged me to create something beautiful to look at.” After dinner, Rico took a snap of my truck in the parking lot. It was dark outside, but that’s all he needed to get the ball rolling. Going forward, we spoke via text and DMs on Instagram. I kicked things off with the above photo of the XL Sport, but I wanted Rico to run with this seed and make it blossom as his own creation. Ideation and Creation AI does come in handy for ideation. ChatGPT These were not working for me. Mr. Culmination Initial color/gradient rendering. Mr. Culmination The color palette of the Jazz disposable cup wasn’t working for me, so I used AI image generation to turn that 1993 Ranger into something akin to my vision. AI did a good job tweaking colors to my commands, even if it butchered the graphics and the truck, likely to avoid copyright issues. I shared the AI photo with Rico, but unfortunately I didn’t make it clear that AI was only intended for the color palette. His work needed to hinge on the original 1993 image, so time was wasted in the miscommunication. People shouldn’t work for free, and I wanted to make up for his wasted efforts. But Rico was extremely generous with his time, suggesting he was fitting me in between jobs. (The whole job set me back around $900, but don’t expect every commissioned graphic designer to be this generous with their talents. Again, nobody should work for free.) Having the unintended extra time was good, as I had another graphic that needed installing. I bought this “Ford” tailgate graphic over 10 years ago for dirt-cheap on eBay, because I hate the F-150-sized, OEM tailgate emblems on the last of these compact Rangers. I was glad to de-badge/repaint the tailgate when the opportunity presented itself, in the form of a hit-and-run in a parking lot. After, the tailgate looked naked, and this decal was perfect. It’s fine on a 2006 F-150,but a Ranger? Mecum Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Turns out this tailgate decal was only for 1993–94 Rangers, just like the side graphics I chose for my project. Perhaps Ford regretted the Taco Bell–themed body sides just as much as it did Ford product leaving the factory without a blue oval emblem affixed to its posterior. Whether that’s true or not is irrelevant, as that notion further cemented my mission. Months passed, and Rico came through with the goods. He took the 1993–94 XL Sport graphics as a foundation, removed the “Sport” verbiage from the doors, changed the colors to a mix of grays and reds, extended the pattern further down the bed, and made it flow to the taillight contouring at the end of the body. This was everything I wanted, and more: Rico made the graphic his own with color gradients never seen in 1993, and added white borders for extra pop on the silver body. I liked his vision and asked him to take it to the next stage of creation. Rico’s first. Sajeev Mehta Rico’s second. Sajeev Mehta Note the white accents on the second. Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Rico obliged, visiting my home with test prints and color swatches to ensure I would be happy with the final product. I decided the red needed to start off bright, worthy of my alma mater (University of Houston). White worked great with the bright red elements, and the gray area was offset with a splash of pure black. Rico initially had more black on the design, but I insisted on gray levels that started at the charcoal present in my truck’s OEM-plus Alcoa wheels. The design was finalized after a few moments looking at colors and test prints in direct sunlight. The final product may not appeal to the general public, but the artist and this particular customer were sold. So the 1993–94 Ranger-inspired design for my truck went to the printers, and I reserved a day for Rico to install his masterpiece. Installation Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Rico was kind enough to do all the work in my garage, so I ensured he remained hydrated while I continued to write for Hagerty Media. Of course, I took breaks to witness the installation process and to photograph it for posterity. Turns out Rico was more invested in the process than I anticipated, because he really embraced this truck’s mission: “This Ranger has many OEM modifications that most people can’t tell. The aim was to make a livery that would be a great conversation starter, and would open the door for an explanation of the modifications presented to the viewer. Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta “The livery had to be done within the original 1993–94 design to keep it as OEM as possible, but I found a way to bring more depth and direction to the shapes. These forms are intended to be sympathetic to the shape of the Ranger’s body. If I do it right, I will create intention and narrative behind every curve, shade, and gradient.” Designing it right is one thing, but getting it on sheetmetal is another. This graphic is quite complex, and therefore not easy to install. Rico spent nearly a full day in my garage, on a day with enough humidity to make installation a challenge. Because this is a continuous design from panel to panel, he said, “a small 0.25-inch error in the front can cause the whole project to be halted or forced to be redone completely.” I suspect Ford’s 1993–94 Ranger graphic is less complicated for this reason; the design changes significantly between the cab and the bed, likely for ease of installation at the factory. Rico made installation harder for himself, but perhaps that’s a mark of an artist who is truly dedicated to his craft. “As each section went on, the truck began to gain more life, especially at the reveal when we removed the masking paper. Seeing the vinyl contour to the curves of the truck just made it look more lively. Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta “I also aimed to create chaos, to keep the design surprising and exciting for the viewer. The bold red colors radiate intense energy but the subtle grays smooth that energy back into the truck. This gives it a more composed look. The look is confident, with a large presence, while not being overly arrogant.” I think he nailed it. This is precisely why I wanted someone like Rico behind the project. I wanted to commission an artist, someone who understands the assignment and isn’t afraid to take my original idea to a higher level. Rico suggested that he always had an idea of how the final product would look, but even he was surprised at how good the graphics look, especially from vantage points you can’t experience on a computer screen. Public Reaction Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta While commissioning custom graphics for my Ranger is my equivalent of buying a red sports car, I genuinely craved the opinions of relevant third parties. The first was my father, who barged out of his house upon my arrival to exclaim, “Wow, did you buy a new truck?”Honestly, I could have stopped there. Dad’s exclamation of surprise and delight was worth every penny, every laborious hour of Rico’s precious time. Then I reached out to my friend Denny, a local who’s made a name for himself with his Ultimate 1980s Garage . I will go on a limb and assume his midlife journey is much like mine. Denny’s love includes bringing Houston’s Rad Era community together without gatekeeping or cliquey drama. One of his events was the perfect place to put my graphics to the test, so I made a point to capitalize on the platform he created. Sajeev Mehta Ford I texted Denny to ask for a prominent spot at his next show, making sure to include a photo of my Ranger and the XL Sport as justification. He actually remembered these graphics when they were new (this only adds more credibility to his arsenal of automotive knowledge). “I thought maybe they did a red version!” He texted back. “This looks sweet!” Retro-graphic approval from Denny is akin to a blessing from Jay Leno, so I arrived at the show early and was allowed to park the Ranger wherever I wanted. It no longer felt wrong to park my humble truck amongst blue-chip cars from the 1980s and 1990s and the latest flights of fancy. Luckily for my ego, the Ranger turned heads to the point that folks walked around it to see the graphic’s full effect. 1993 Ford Ranger XL Sport Reddit | evannovoa Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. Sajeev Mehta I think Rico’s mission to make my truck a “great conversation starter” is fulfilled. While I lacked the nerve to solicit opinions from strangers, I did enjoy the overwhelmingly positive feedback from my friends in attendance. It was a diverse group: men and women, Generation X down to Generation Z, and fans of all automotive marques. However, I soon craved more validation. My brother loves cars like his sibling (his influence is why I’m writing here), but he’s a tough customer. He had remained silent for weeks on the matter of the Ranger’s graphics, so upon his arrival at Denny’s show, I flatly asked for his opinion. I set the tone with a little self-deprecation. “So, how much or how little do you hate the graphics I put on the Ranger?” “No, no, I think it works well for you,” he dryly remarked. Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Sajeev Mehta Later on, he generously let me switch keys so I could drive his car show–appropriate sports car back to town. Too bad I wasn’t wise to his game. You see, he was playing 4-D chess. Less than a minute after he slid behind the wheel of the Ranger, a showgoer and his son finished their walkaround and complimented him on “his” truck. “Hey, that’s a really nice Ranger!” My brother thanked the man with a big smile on his face. With that, he let out the clutch and drove away. As the Bassani exhaust’s baritone note floated off into the horizon, I was left in a void of disappointment. I’ve been waiting since 2011 to get such a remark from a stranger. The key to his off-the-shelf sports car felt heavy in my pocket, like an albatross around my neck. I was crestfallen. Oh dear, I thought. I fear a second midlife crisis is approaching… The post How to Solve a Midlife Crisis with the Car You Already Have appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Doximity to Acquire Amion, Leader in Physician Scheduling
body_text: Amion manages nearly 200k physician schedules at thousands of hospitals including 18 of the top 20 SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 8, 2022--Doximity, Inc. (NYSE: DOCS), the leading digital platform for U.S. medical professionals, today announced that it has acquired Amion, a leading on-call physician scheduling site. Amion manages nearly 200,000 physician schedules at thousands of hospitals, including 18 of the top 20. ”We’re excited to partner with founder Stuart Karon and the Amion team to expand our physician cloud platform,” said Jeff Tangney, CEO and co-founder at Doximity. “Scheduling enhances our collaboration suite and will grow engagement across all our businesses.” “For 24 years, Amion fostered a micro-company model to maximize operational efficiency,” said Stuart Karon, CEO and founder at Amion. “We’re excited to add Doximity’s growth gene to our DNA. Formalizing our decade-long partnership will bring great new tools to many more physicians.” The transaction is expected to close April 1, 2022. About Amion Amion is a leading web and mobile on-call scheduling and messaging application for hospitals and physicians. With Amion, groups build balanced, equitable schedules which they post on Amion.com for staff to view and sync work shifts to personal calendars. The mobile application combines scheduling with communication and lets staff submit special requests and swap shifts. Amion founder and CEO Stuart Karon developed an early version of the application in 1998 to help his wife Jodi Wenger, MD, then a chief pediatric resident, build schedules for her large residency training program. Amion is based in the Boston area. About Doximity Founded in 2010, Doximity is the leading digital platform for U.S. medical professionals. The company's network members include over 80% of U.S. physicians across all specialties and practice areas. Doximity provides its verified clinical membership with digital tools built for medicine, enabling them to collaborate with colleagues, stay up to date with the latest medical news and research, manage their careers and conduct virtual patient visits. Doximity's mission is to help doctors be more productive so they can provide better care for their patients. For more information visit Doximity.com . Doximity Media Contact: pr@doximity.com

title: Powered by PacBio: Selected publications from April – June 2026
summary: In this second quarterly edition of Powered by PacBio, we highlight three publications from April, May, and June.
body_text: This quarter’s publications are showing us where genomics is headed: from incomplete views of the genome toward comprehensive, genome-wide analysis. Across population genomics, clinical whole-genome sequencing, and medical genetics, researchers are increasingly showing that long-read sequencing is becoming foundational for the next generation of genomic discovery and precision medicine. In this second quarterly edition of Powered by PacBio , we highlight three publications from April, May, and June that show this transition. They include a landmark Chinese population pangenome paper published in Nature , a clinical study showing how HiFi whole-genome sequencing can consolidate multiple genetic tests into a single assay for reproductive medicine, and a perspective introducing the concept of Near-Perfect Genome Sequencing (NPGS) as a roadmap for the future of medical genetics. Keep reading for a closer look at these featured publications from April through June 2026. Jump to topic: Population genomics | Whole genome sequencing | Medical genetics Population genomics The 1000 Chinese Pangenome empowers medical and population genetics In this Nature paper , researchers from China describe “1,116 diploid genome assemblies (55 de novo and 1,061 pangenome-informed) as part of the 1KCP [1000 Chinese Pangenome] project,” creating one of the largest population-specific pangenome resources to date. Key highlights: Researchers built a pangenome containing “405.3 million base pairs of sequences absent from the current references GRCh38 and CHM13,” including “26.2 million base pairs of functional genic and predicted regulatory elements,” while cataloging “a full spectrum of genetic variation.” This resource enabled “detailed characterization of multiscale genic variations relevant to medical genetics,” including gene-altering SVs, tandem repeat expansions, gene cluster variation, and HLA haplotypes. The authors conclude: “As the costs of long-read sequencing continue to fall, we anticipate that this strategy will be increasingly adopted in large cohorts to advance precision medicine and benefit human health.” Conclusion: This study shows the power of HiFi sequencing for population-scale genomics. Even with relatively low-coverage Sequel II data, researchers generated a Nature publication and a landmark resource for medical genetics. With today’s Revio system and SPRQ-Nx chemistry, building comprehensive population pangenomes is becoming even more scalable, cost-effective, and practical for large national genomics initiatives. Whole genome sequencing Using HiFi Long-Read Whole Genome Sequencing to Enhance Diagnosis in Patients with Subfertility and/or Recurrent Pregnancy Loss In this multi-center study , researchers from 14 institutions led by KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (Singapore) demonstrate that “a single long-read genome sequencing test can consolidate multiple genetic investigations and uncover clinically relevant causes in couples with unexplained subfertility and recurrent pregnancy loss.” Key highlights: The authors note that “existing workflows require sequential testing and may miss complex genomic variants,” leaving “many couples … undiagnosed after multiple conventional genetic tests.” Using HiFi whole-genome sequencing in 84 individuals , the study found “1 in 10 couples harboring a clinically significant variant” that “would directly benefit from genetic testing.” HiFi sequencing also improved diagnostic confidence. For couples carrying “one pathogenic variant in recessively inherited genes,” long reads enabled researchers to “rule out any other rare coding and/or noncoding variants in the second allele, providing greater certainty.” Even when no causative variant was identified, the authors note that “comprehensively ruling out known genetic causes is also valuable information.” Beyond the primary indication, “26 individuals were identified to be carriers of a recessive genetic disease, and 1 individual has a secondary finding,” highlighting the broader value of genome-wide testing. Long-read sequencing also resolved complex inheritance. In one individual, “two disease-causing variants in the same gene” were shown through phasing to reside on the same allele, reducing the need for additional testing. Conclusion: This first publication from the HiFi Solves Subfertility Consortium in APAC adds to growing evidence that a single HiFi genome can replace multiple sequential genetic tests. By consolidating assays while improving confidence, HiFi WGS offers a streamlined approach for investigating unexplained subfertility and recurrent pregnancy loss, bringing comprehensive reproductive genomics closer to routine clinical assessments. Medical genetics Near-perfect genome sequencing in medical genetics In this perspective , researchers from Radboud University Medical Center introduce Near-Perfect Genome Sequencing (NPGS) , proposing that “long-read genome sequencing constitutes the foundational layer of the NPGS framework.” Key highlights: The authors describe how “short-read sequencing technologies … carry well-documented blind spots,” including highly homologous regions, tandem repeats, segmental duplications, large and complex SVs, invisible base modifications, and a lack of variant phasing. As a result, they argue that “the term ‘whole-genome sequencing’ is therefore a misnomer in clinical practice.” To overcome these limitations, they propose that “long-read genome sequencing should be considered as one pillar of a broader technological convergence encompassing diploid genome assembly, pangenome references and AI-driven variant interpretation,” collectively termed Near-Perfect Genome Sequencing (NPGS). The paper highlights NPGS applications across postnatal constitutional diagnostics , where it “holds the greatest potential to consolidate the existing diagnostic toolkit under a one-test paradigm,” as well as oncology and population screening , where it addresses limitations of current short-read approaches. The authors also present a three-stage roadmap outlining the path from current practice to routine NPGS implementation. Conclusion: “NPGS carries the potential to subsume the existing diagnostic toolkit of medical genetics within a single unified framework, fundamentally reshaping the genetic diagnostics landscape over the coming decades.” Conclusion: This paper offers a compelling vision for the future of medical genetics—one built on long-read sequencing as its foundation. By combining HiFi sequencing with diploid assemblies, pangenomes, and AI-driven interpretation, the NPGS framework moves beyond incremental improvements toward a truly comprehensive view of the genome. As these technologies continue to mature together, HiFi is positioned to serve as the foundation for the next generation of genomic medicine. Ready to make discoveries of your own? These studies are great examples of where our field is headed. Population-scale pangenomes, comprehensive whole-genome sequencing, and integrated long-read analysis show us everything from how to build more representative reference resources to how long-read sequencing is helping to establish new standards for genomic medicine. We’ll be back next this fall with another collection of standout publications showcasing how researchers around the world are putting PacBio technology to work. Ready to see how you can use HiFi sequencing for your next project? Let’s get started .

title: 9 Shopify Alternatives for Building Your Online Store
summary: Compare 9 Shopify alternatives, from cheaper hosted platforms to building a store you fully own. See what each one really costs before you switch.
body_text: Shopify makes it easy to launch an online store, but its true cost can grow quickly. Transaction fees, paid apps, premium themes, and development work can add up, while template and platform limits may leave sellers wanting more control over their storefront, code, and data. This guide compares nine genuine Shopify alternatives, from cheaper hosted platforms to open-source and build-your-own options. We’ll look at their costs, limitations, technical requirements, ownership models, and best use cases to help you find the right fit for your store. Why Sellers Look for a Shopify Alternative Shopify works well for sellers who want to launch quickly without managing hosting, security, or checkout infrastructure themselves. The reasons people start looking for cheaper alternatives to Shopify usually become clearer as sales, app requirements, and customization needs grow. The most common cost concerns are: Transaction fees: On the US Basic plan, standard online card rates start at 2.9% plus 30¢. Sellers using an outside payment provider can also pay a 2% Shopify transaction fee on top of that provider’s processing charges. Paid apps: Reviews, subscriptions, upsells, advanced shipping, and other functions may require separate tools. For example, Recharge Starter costs $99 per month plus 1.49% and 19¢ per transaction, while Loox Convert costs $49.99 per month. Those two plans alone total nearly $150 per month before other apps are added. Shopify’s current pricing confirms the additional third-party transaction fee, while its App Store shows how quickly individual subscriptions can stack up. Merchants raise the same concern in public discussions. In a Shopify Community thread about app dependence, one seller described repeatedly paying “$5 to $15 a month” for small functions they believed should be built in. An app developer offered the other side: apps can be more practical than hiring a developer, although managing too many can become a “maintenance nightmare.” Control is the other major issue. Sellers may eventually want more freedom over: Storefront layouts and branding Checkout and custom product workflows Backend functionality and integrations Their code, hosting, and ability to move providers Shopify themes can be customized, but more specialized functionality may require Liquid development, an app, or custom development. Shopify’s plan comparison currently lists checkout customization as limited on Basic, Grow, and Advanced, with full checkout customization offered on Plus. The r/ecommerce thread on Shopify alternatives reflects both sides of the decision. Some merchants favor WooCommerce for deeper customization, control over hosting, and the ability to move their data between providers. Others argue that Shopify remains cost-effective because its simplicity lets new sellers focus on making sales rather than maintaining a website. Migration can still create friction. Shopify lets merchants export products and orders and download theme files, but a theme download does not include products, pages, blog posts, images, or other store content. Moving platforms may therefore require transferring several datasets, replacing apps, and rebuilding parts of the storefront. None of this makes Shopify a poor choice, but alternatives become more appealing when lower recurring costs, custom functionality, or greater ownership matter more than the convenience of a managed platform. How We Evaluated These Shopify Alternatives We compared each platform using the factors that matter most once a store moves beyond the launch stage: Real cost: Monthly plans, platform transaction fees, required apps, hosting, and other add-ons Ownership: How much control sellers have over their store, code, and data Customization: How far the storefront, checkout, and backend workflows can be changed Ease of use: The technical skill and setup time required Scalability: How well the platform handles more traffic, products, integrations, and operational complexity Support: The quality of documentation, customer service, and available developer help There is no single best choice among Shopify competitors. A hosted builder may be the right fit for a seller who values speed and simplicity, while an open-source or build-your-own platform may suit a business that needs greater flexibility and ownership. The best alternative depends on the store’s current size, technical resources, budget, and long-term goals. The 9 Best Shopify Alternatives The best alternatives to Shopify range from simple hosted builders to open-source platforms with much more flexibility. Some are designed for sellers who want a faster or cheaper setup, while others are better suited to businesses that need custom functionality, stronger design control, or greater ownership. The options below are reviewed using the same criteria: features, ease of use, pricing, transaction fees, ownership, scalability, and overall fit. This makes it easier to compare not just what each platform offers, but which type of seller it is actually built for. 1. BigCommerce Best for: growing business-to-consumer (B2C) or business-to-business (B2B) stores that need more commerce features built into the platform. BigCommerce is a hosted software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform that manages hosting, security, checkout, and software updates. It supports standard storefronts, headless builds, B2B selling, and multiple stores from one account, making it suitable for established retailers, wholesalers, and multi-brand businesses. Key features: Customizable themes and a drag-and-drop page builder Product, order, and multi-location inventory management One-page checkout and support for multiple payment providers Marketplace and social-channel integrations Multi-Storefront controls for different brands or regions B2B tools such as company accounts, price lists, and quotes Ease of use: A standard store can be launched without coding. Advanced theme changes, unusual product workflows, and headless storefronts generally require technical knowledge or developer support. What users like: BigCommerce has a 4.2/5 rating from 579 G2 reviews, with users commonly praising its built-in features, integrations, and ability to manage complex catalogs. Its Trustpilot rating is lower at 1.2/5 from 455 reviews, where complaints often focus on billing, price increases, and customer support. Limitations: The admin interface and page builder can feel less intuitive than simpler hosted platforms. Stores are also moved to higher-priced plans when they cross certain sales thresholds. Pricing and fees: Core starts at $39 monthly or $29 per month annually. Growth starts at $105 or $79, while Scale starts at $399 or $299. BigCommerce does not add transaction fees when an embedded payment provider is used, but outside providers can trigger fees of 2%, 1%, or 0.6%, depending on the plan. Ownership and scalability: Merchants can export their data and download theme code, but the commerce backend remains hosted by BigCommerce. The platform can support large catalogs, multiple channels, B2B operations, and regional storefronts. Best fit: Established sellers that need stronger native B2B, catalog, and multi-store capabilities. Why it is a good Shopify alternative: BigCommerce can reduce dependence on paid apps by including more advanced commerce functions natively, although its revenue-based pricing remains an important tradeoff. 2. WooCommerce Best for: sellers who want full control and are comfortable managing WordPress. WooCommerce is a free, open-source ecommerce plugin for self-hosted WordPress sites. Merchants choose hosting, themes, payment providers, and extensions while retaining control of the store’s code and data. Key features: Product, inventory, order, tax, and shipping management Customizable WordPress themes and checkout More than 140 payment gateway integrations Support for physical products, downloads, subscriptions, and bookings Extensions for marketing, analytics, and multichannel selling Ease of use: Installing WooCommerce on WordPress is straightforward, but setup is more involved than Shopify. Merchants must manage hosting, backups, security, updates, and plugin compatibility or pay someone to do it. What users like: WooCommerce has a 4.4/5 rating from 1,270 G2 reviews, with users praising its customization, WordPress integration, and extension ecosystem. Its Trustpilot rating is 2.3/5 from 141 reviews, where complaints often concern support, technical issues, and paid extensions. Limitations: Plugin conflicts, updates, security, and performance require active management. Costs can rise when a store needs premium extensions, stronger hosting, or developer help. Reddit sellers also praise its flexibility while warning about the learning curve. Pricing and fees: The core plugin is free, making it a free Shopify alternative. Hosting, domains, themes, and extensions cost extra. WooCommerce adds no platform transaction fee; US WooPayments card processing is 2.9% plus 30¢. Ownership and scalability: Merchants own the code and data and can move between hosts. WooCommerce can support complex stores, but production readiness depends on hosting, optimization, and plugin quality. Best fit: WordPress users and technical teams that value customization and ownership. Why it is a good Shopify alternative: WooCommerce removes platform lock-in and per-sale platform fees, but shifts more technical responsibility to the seller. 3. Wix Best for: small stores that want a fast, flexible no-code launch. Wix is a hosted SaaS website builder with built-in ecommerce, hosting, security, and business tools. It suits beginners and small businesses that want more design freedom than a rigid storefront template without managing infrastructure. Key features: Drag-and-drop editor, AI builder, and 2,000+ templates Product, inventory, order, shipping, and tax management Abandoned-cart recovery and back-in-stock alerts Selling through Amazon, eBay, Etsy, TikTok, and social channels Wix Payments, PayPal, Stripe, and 80+ regional payment providers Online and in-person inventory syncing through Wix point-of-sale (POS) Ease of use: A basic store can be launched without code, although the number of editor options may initially feel overwhelming. Advanced custom functions can be added through Wix’s developer tools. What users like: Wix has a 4.2/5 rating from 1,871 G2 reviews, where users commonly praise its ease of use and broad feature set. Its Trustpilot score is 3.5/5 from 28,486 reviews, with positive feedback on design tools but recurring complaints about billing and support. Limitations: Wix can support substantial catalogs, but complex B2B operations and highly customized checkout workflows may outgrow its standard tools. A Wix website also cannot be hosted outside Wix because it relies on proprietary platform technology. Pricing and fees: Ecommerce begins on the Core plan at roughly $29 per month on annual billing. Business is about $39 and Business Elite about $159, although pricing varies by location. Wix charges no separate platform transaction fee; standard US card processing through Wix Payments is 2.9% plus 30¢. Ownership and scalability: Merchants own their content and can export store data, but not the complete working website. Wix is production-ready for small and midsize stores, with enterprise options for larger organizations. Best fit: New or growing sellers that want design flexibility without technical maintenance. Why it is a good Shopify alternative: Wix offers a simpler design experience and no added platform transaction fee while still providing core ecommerce and multichannel tools. 4. Squarespace Best for: design-led brands with a focused product catalog. Squarespace is a hosted SaaS website builder known for polished templates and strong visual presentation. Its ecommerce tools are built into the same system as its website, blogging, scheduling, invoicing, and marketing features. Key features: Professionally designed, mobile-responsive templates Drag-and-drop storefront and product-page editing Unlimited physical products and services Inventory, order, discount, and customer-account tools Abandoned-checkout recovery and product subscriptions Instagram and Facebook promotion, POS, and Google Shopping support Ease of use: Squarespace is one of the easier platforms for creating a professional-looking store without code. Its editor is approachable for beginners, although unusual layouts or custom commerce workflows may require Cascading Style Sheets (CSS), code injection, or extensions. What users like: Squarespace has a 4.4/5 rating from 1,132 G2 reviews, with users praising its templates and ease of use. Its Trustpilot score is 3.3/5 from 4,369 reviews, where experiences with support are mixed and some users report billing or customization frustrations. Limitations: Squarespace offers less backend flexibility and fewer deep commerce integrations than Shopify. Stores can accept only one currency at a time, and the platform is less suitable for large, operationally complex catalogs. Pricing and fees: Current US annual pricing starts at $19 per month for Basic, followed by Core at $29, Plus at $49, and Advanced at $99. Basic adds a 2% online-store transaction fee, while Core, Plus, and Advanced charge 0%. Payment-processing fees still apply. Squarespace has no permanent free plan, but it offers a 14-day trial. Ownership and scalability: Products and orders can be exported, but some product images, reviews, and other details do not transfer through the standard comma-separated values (CSV) file. The storefront and backend remain tied to Squarespace. Best fit: Creators and lifestyle brands that prioritize presentation over complex commerce operations. Why it is a good Shopify alternative: Squarespace combines attractive design and commerce tools with less app dependence, making it a strong choice for smaller, brand-focused stores. 5. Webflow Best for: design-focused teams that want precise control over the storefront experience. Webflow is a hosted visual-development platform with ecommerce functionality. It lets designers build custom storefronts, carts, and checkout pages without being confined to a conventional theme, while still offering access to custom Hypertext Markup Language (HTML), CSS, and JavaScript. Key features: Visual control over product pages, carts, and checkout Product, category, variant, inventory, and order management Physical, digital, service, and membership products Stripe, PayPal, Apple Pay, and browser-based payments Custom shipping rules and automatic tax calculations Content management system (CMS), animations, search engine optimization (SEO) controls, and custom-code support Ease of use: Webflow provides more design freedom than most no-code builders, but it has a steeper learning curve. Sellers unfamiliar with web layout concepts such as containers, classes, breakpoints, and responsive design may need training or professional help. What users like: Webflow has a 4.4/5 rating from 984 G2 reviews, with users frequently praising its design flexibility, CMS, and ability to translate design intent into a working site. Its Trustpilot score is 1.5/5 from 228 reviews, where recent complaints focus on pricing, complexity, bugs, and support. Limitations: Webflow’s native commerce tools are less extensive than Shopify’s for multichannel sales, advanced inventory, and complex retail operations. Product limits also range from 500 to 15,000 items depending on the plan. Pricing and fees: Standard costs $29 per month annually and adds a 2% Webflow transaction fee. Plus costs $74 and Advanced costs $212, with no platform transaction fee on either. Stripe or PayPal processing charges apply separately. Ownership and scalability: Paid Workspace users can export HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets, but ecommerce databases, products, checkout, and other commerce functions are excluded. Products can be exported separately by CSV, so moving a complete functioning store still requires rebuilding the backend. Best fit: Design-led brands with relatively straightforward commerce requirements. Why it is a good Shopify alternative: Webflow offers much deeper visual control than a standard Shopify theme, but trades some operational commerce depth for that freedom.

Beasley Media Group’s 97.5 THE FANATIC Crowns a New Era & Becomes 97.5 LEBRON… HOME OF KING JAMES
summary: Philadelphia's flagship radio home of the 76ers celebrates the arrival of LeBron James with a temporary station rebrand
body_text: Philadelphia’s flagship radio home of the 76ers celebrates the arrival of LeBron James with a temporary station rebrand Philadelphia, PA (July 24, 2026) : Following today’s historic announcement that LeBron James is joining the Philadelphia 76ers, 97.5 The Fanatic is celebrating in true Philadelphia fashion. Effective immediately, the station will temporarily rebrand as “97.5 LeBron… Home of King James!” honoring one of the most significant moments in franchise history. The temporary rebrand will be featured across the station’s on-air imaging, website, app, and social media platforms as Philadelphia welcomes one of the greatest players the game has ever seen. Throughout the day, listeners will hear new station IDs proclaiming “97.5 LeBron… Home of King James!” while The Fanatic’s hosts provide complete coverage of the blockbuster signing, including breaking news, fan reaction, exclusive interviews, press conference coverage, roster analysis, and what this landmark move means for the future of the 76ers. “As the flagship station of the Philadelphia 76ers, we knew we had to celebrate this moment in a way that matched its magnitude,” said Paul Blake, Vice President and Market Manager of Beasley Media Group Philadelphia. “This is one of those rare days that changes the course of a franchise and energizes an entire city. Becoming ‘97.5 LeBron… Home of King James!’ is our way of celebrating alongside Sixers fans everywhere.” “These are the moments sports radio is built for,” said Scott Masteller, Program Director of 97.5 The Fanatic. “Philadelphia has been waiting for this day, and every conversation is about LeBron and the Sixers. From the first show this morning through the final segment tonight, we’re bringing fans everything they need to know about one of the biggest stories in NBA history.” As the official flagship station of the Philadelphia 76ers, 97.5 LeBron… Home of King James! will deliver comprehensive coverage throughout the day and beyond, featuring breaking news, exclusive interviews, fan interaction, expert analysis, and complete coverage of one of the most impactful acquisitions in NBA history. As the official flagship station of the Philadelphia 76ers, 97.5 LeBron… Home of King James! will deliver comprehensive coverage of the teams and stories that matter most to Philadelphia sports fans. For updates, visit 975TheFanatic.com and follow @975TheFanatic across all social media platforms. Note: 97.5 LeBron… Home of King James is a temporary news promotion. No affiliation, sponsorship, or endorsement by LeBron James is implied.
